title: Daily Financial Workflow, Controls, and Reconciliation

sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe the daily financial workflow of a medical office, including charge entry, payment posting, end-of-day balancing, and deposits.
- Explain the purpose of financial controls and the reconciliation process, including segregation of duties, receipts, and bank reconciliation.
- Recognize common error and fraud risks in billing and cash handling and apply prevention and escalation practices.
- Demonstrate accurate recording and reconciliation of cash, check, credit card, and insurance payments within scope of practice.
- Identify the medical office assistant's role in safeguarding funds, following policies, and reporting discrepancies appropriately.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Reconciliation is like checking that the money in your piggy bank matches the list of coins you wrote down. If they do not match, you figure out what is missing or extra.

### Question 2

A day sheet is like a class attendance and lunch-money list rolled into one: it shows everything that was charged and every payment that came in that day.

### Question 3

The superbill is like a restaurant receipt that lists everything the patient received at the visit, so the office knows what to charge for.

### Question 4

Closing the day is like finishing a homework checklist: do the problems (charges), mark them correct (payments), check your work (reconcile), then turn it in (deposit).

### Question 5

Putting money in the bank right away is like putting your lunch in the fridge instead of leaving it on the counter—it is safer and fresher.

### Question 6

When someone pays you, you write it down and give them a receipt right away—like a lemonade stand writing down every cup sold.

### Question 7

The change fund is like starting a cash register with exactly $50 so that at the end of the day you can tell exactly how much was taken in.

### Question 8

Settling a batch is like closing out the cash register at a store so the card machine sends all of the day's sales to the bank at once.

### Question 9

Posting a payment is like putting a letter in the right mailbox—each payment must go to the exact patient it belongs to, or the account gets mixed up.

### Question 10

Collecting a copay at check-in is like paying for your movie ticket before you enter the theater—you pay for the visit when you arrive.

### Question 11

An unapplied payment is like getting a letter without a name on it—you set it safely aside and figure out who it belongs to instead of guessing.

### Question 12

A patient ledger is like a running scoreboard for one patient's account, showing what was charged, what was paid, and what is still owed.

### Question 13

A bounced check is like a gift card that turns out to be empty—you have to undo the payment and ask for the money another way.

### Question 14

Handling a mailed payment is like sorting the day's mail into the right cubbies and then taking everything to the bank together.

### Question 15

Petty cash is like a small jar of money for buying office stamps; every time you take money out, you drop in a receipt to prove what it was for.

### Question 16

You put all the items on your shopping list before you subtract your coupons, so you know the true total before anything is taken off.

### Question 17

Your balance is like money owed on a bill: start with what was charged, then subtract what was paid and any discounts, and whatever is left is what you still owe.

### Question 18

Daily tasks are like brushing your teeth every night, while monthly tasks are like a monthly checkup that looks at the bigger picture.

### Question 19

An aging report is like a stack of bills sorted by how overdue each one is, so you know which ones to chase first.

### Question 20

At the end of the day you put your money in a locked safe, just like locking your bike instead of leaving it on the sidewalk.

### Question 21

Segregation of duties is like having one person bake the cookies and a different person count the money, so no one person can take a cookie and hide it.

### Question 22

You would not let the same person both grade the test and write the answer key—separating the jobs helps catch mistakes and cheating.

### Question 23

Prenumbered receipts are like pages in a book with numbers in order—if page 7 is missing, you know something was torn out.

### Question 24

Writing "For Deposit Only" is like labeling your lunch bag with your name—it tells everyone this check is only allowed to go to the bank.

### Question 25

Dual control is like two hall monitors both counting the fundraiser money so nobody can slip a bill into their pocket unnoticed.

### Question 26

You keep money in a locked box, not out on the table, so only the right people can reach it.

### Question 27

Writing down money the moment you get it is like putting a leash on a puppy right away—wait too long and it might wander off.

### Question 28

A bank reconciliation is like checking your homework answers against the teacher's answer key to see why any of them are different.

### Question 29

An outstanding check is like a letter you mailed that is still in the mail truck—you already count it, but the bank has not received it yet.

### Question 30

A deposit in transit is like money you put in the night-drop box after hours—you wrote it down, but the bank will not show it until the next day.

### Question 31

When your check is still in the mail, you subtract it from the bank's number to line up with what your own notebook says.

### Question 32

If you accidentally write 89 instead of 98, the two numbers are 9 apart—a little trick accountants use to spot swapped digits fast.

### Question 33

If the store refunds you less than you expected, you read the receipt to see why before deciding anything—the remittance advice is that receipt.

### Question 34

An audit trail is like a security camera on the cash register—it shows who did what and when, so nothing can happen in secret.

### Question 35

Having your own login is like having your own locker with your own combination, so everyone is responsible for their own things.

### Question 36

Fixing a mistake on an official record is like asking the teacher to initial a correction—someone in charge has to approve it so the change is honest.

### Question 37

Giving money back is like returning a library book—you need a record of what is being returned and a librarian's approval before it is checked back in.

### Question 38

A good petty cash system is like a class treasurer who keeps every receipt and counts the money jar every week.

### Question 39

A surprise audit is like a pop quiz—because you know it could happen anytime, you stay prepared and honest every day.

### Question 40

Having one friend open the envelopes and another write down the money is like a two-person check so neither can slip a check into their pocket.

### Question 41

Erasing what a patient owes is like a store clerk deciding on their own to give away free merchandise—only a manager can approve that.

### Question 42

If two receipts disagree, you do not tear one up—you lay them side by side and find the missing transaction.

### Question 43

Counting the day's money is like checking that the coins in your jar match the list and the deposit slip you wrote.

### Question 44

If one person is the only one who touches, writes down, and double-checks the money, it is like the same kid grading their own test—too easy to hide a mistake or a trick.

### Question 45

Missing receipt numbers are like pages torn out of a numbered notebook—you know something was removed and needs to be found.

### Question 46

If one person keeps quietly erasing small amounts from lots of accounts, it is like someone nibbling cookies from the jar—each piece is small but it adds up.

### Question 47

Embezzlement is like a babysitter who is trusted with the cookie money but secretly keeps some of it instead of turning it all in.

### Question 48

Skimming is like taking a cookie from the jar before anyone counts them, so the count still looks right.

### Question 49

Lapping is like borrowing from tomorrow's allowance to replace money you took today, so the jar always looks full but is never quite right.

### Question 50

If your class money jar comes up short, you tell the teacher instead of quietly adding your own coins—so the real reason can be found.

### Question 51

Changing the numbers to make them match is like fixing a wobbly table by pretending it is level—you cover up the problem instead of fixing it.

### Question 52

If the register does not add up, you count again slowly, and if it still does not match, you get the manager—you never just erase the numbers.

### Question 53

A card number is like a secret password—you never write it down where others can see it or keep it in an unlocked drawer.

### Question 54

A signed blank check is like giving someone a blank permission slip with your name already on it—they could write in anything.

### Question 55

Office money is like the school's field-trip fund—it belongs to everyone and can never be used for your own snacks, even if you plan to pay it back.

### Question 56

If you think someone is breaking the rules, you tell a trusted adult in charge—you do not yell at them or tell everyone in the neighborhood.

### Question 57

Before giving back money, you check the person's ID and the paperwork, just like the library checks your card before handing over a book.

### Question 58

Double-checking the amount is like proofreading a number before you hit send—catching a swapped digit now saves a big fix later.

### Question 59

Money is like ice cream—the longer it sits out, the more likely it is to disappear, so you put it away quickly.

### Question 60

Checking your homework every day is like catching a wrong answer right away, instead of finding out at the end of the year that you were doing it wrong all along.

### Question 61

A strange check on the bank statement is like finding a charge on your account you did not make—you tell a grown-up in charge right away.

### Question 62

An anonymous tip line is like a suggestion box where you can slip a note without signing your name, so you feel safe speaking up.

### Question 63

It is easier to keep a secret alone than to get two people to keep the same secret, so splitting the jobs makes sneaky behavior harder.

### Question 64

You lock your locker when you walk away, even for a minute, so no one can reach inside—the cash drawer is the same.

### Question 65

"For Deposit Only" is like writing 'this package goes to the office safe' on a box, so no one else can open it.

### Question 66

You compare your deposit slip to the bank's list, like matching the money you put in your piggy bank to the note your parents wrote down.

### Question 67

A voided check is like a test answer you crossed out—you keep the paper to show what happened, but you never use that answer space again.

### Question 68

If you start with $100 in the register and take in $540 more, the register should hold $640 at the end—start plus what came in.

### Question 69

Start with what you charged ($3,000), subtract what was paid ($1,800) and any discounts ($400), and $800 is what is still owed.

### Question 70

Money showing up in the bank is only half the job—you still have to write down which patient it belongs to, like labeling every jar you fill.

### Question 71

Getting paid at the door is like selling lemonade for cash instead of running a tab you have to chase down later.

### Question 72

A contractual adjustment is the discount the insurance company already agreed to, while a write-off is the office deciding to forgive a bill.

### Question 73

Money from a patient goes into that patient's own piggy bank in the records, not into someone else's jar.

### Question 74

Accounts receivable is like a list of IOUs the practice is still waiting to collect from patients and insurance companies.

### Question 75

If the money jar is short, you write down what is missing and tell the person in charge—you do not secretly refill it and pretend nothing happened.

### Question 76

To catch someone juggling payments, you need a second person checking the money against the receipts every day—like two referees watching one game.

### Question 77

Money goes straight into a locked box, like putting your wallet in a locker instead of leaving it on a bench.

### Question 78

The payment log is like a class roster of every dollar that walked in the door, so you can check the list against the money at day's end.

### Question 79

Collusion is like two hall monitors secretly agreeing to split the fundraiser money, so the usual checks between them stop working.

### Question 80

Daily closing is like tidying your room each night; month-end is like a big monthly clean where you check every drawer and closet.

### Question 81

Good money rules are like a fair referee—they make sure everyone's payment is counted right, so patients can trust the office.

### Question 82

If an adult tells you to change the numbers to make them look right, you say no and tell someone in charge—because making up numbers is never okay.

### Question 83

Extra money in the register is like finding an extra cookie in the jar—you tell an adult because it means something was counted wrong.

### Question 84

Add up every kind of money—bills, checks, and card swipes—the way you count all your birthday money together in one total.

### Question 85

The assistant is like a careful scorekeeper who writes down every point correctly and calls over the referee when something looks wrong.
